question: What does research reveal about how students actually use generative AI when unsupervised — as distinct from how they report using it?
answer:
The gap between what students say and what they do with generative AI is one of the most methodologically revealing puzzles in current educational research — and the evidence, while still accumulating, is already sharp enough to disturb several comfortable assumptions.

The baseline picture from self-report surveys is striking in its own right. By early 2025, 92 percent of UK undergraduate students reported using AI in some form, up from 66 percent the year before, with 88 percent having used generative AI specifically for assessments — more than doubling the figure of 53 percent recorded in 2024. On the surface, this looks like candour at scale. Yet self-report surveys have a well-documented tendency both to overstate socially approved behaviours and to understate stigmatised ones, and the picture becomes considerably more complicated when researchers move beyond questionnaires.

The most consequential finding in recent empirical work comes from studies that examine behavioural logs and interaction traces rather than student testimony. Survey-based studies offer limited insight into how students actually integrate AI into their workflows; one study examining the course-taking behaviour of 70 undergraduate students using behavioural and content-based measures found that 20 percent heavily relied on AI chatbots to complete all written assignments in a philosophy course, between 41 and 70 percent showed at least one instance of "concerning AI usage," and — most strikingly — more than half of those exhibiting clear AI usage patterns denied doing so, raising serious questions about the reliability of self-reports. That last figure is the crux: the self-reporting mechanism, the dominant method in most current research, appears to systematically conceal a substantial share of actual use.

The underreporting is not random. Several studies note that students may underreport AI use due to institutional and ethical pressures. Much of the existing research relies on surveys and interviews, which may underestimate the extent and nature of AI use; few studies document interaction logs, screen recordings, or revision trajectories that reveal how learners actually operationalise AI tools during authentic writing tasks. The methodology gap is therefore not merely academic: it means that the field's dominant evidentiary base — the large-N survey — is structurally ill-suited to the very question it is most often used to answer.

What does emerge when researchers do probe more closely is a taxonomy of rationalisation. A CHI 2025 study on undisclosed use found that when students chose not to disclose their AI use, they avoided disclosure because they feared social judgement (54 percent), feared penalties (44 percent), wanted a competitive advantage (39 percent), or acknowledged it was cheating (37 percent) — yet most justified non-disclosure by arguing it harmed no one, that AI was analogous to other accepted tools like Grammarly, or that instructors themselves used AI to create assignments. Most students who hid their AI use reported not feeling afraid, stressed, or guilty about the non-disclosure. This affective flatness is analytically important: it suggests that for many students, undisclosed AI use has ceased to feel like a transgression requiring suppression, and has instead been reclassified, privately, as something closer to a neutral tool choice.

That reclassification is partly explained by the moral architecture students bring to the question. A survey of 401 students at major US universities found that students' ethical beliefs — not institutional policies — are the strongest predictors of both perceived misconduct and actual AI use in writing; policy awareness had no significant effect on ethical judgements or behaviour. Students who believed AI writing was cheating were substantially less likely to engage with it, while many students did not treat AI use in learning activities as an extension of conventional cheating such as plagiarism, but rather as a distinct category of academic conduct. Institutional rules, in other words, are largely bypassed by the student's own prior moral framework, which varies considerably across individuals.

The deeper patterns of use, when observed rather than reported, reveal a more diverse landscape than the binary of "cheating versus not cheating" captures. Contrary to fears about widespread academic dishonesty, students at one elite US liberal arts college — where over 80 percent now use generative AI for academic purposes — use AI more for augmentation (61 percent) than automation (42 percent). The augmentation category — using AI to clarify concepts, pressure-test arguments, or overcome writer's block — overlaps significantly with what has historically been considered acceptable academic support. Students primarily value generative AI for its ability to enhance time efficiency in concept clarification, boost confidence, and improve the overall quality of their academic work. These self-reported motivations are plausible, but they coexist with the behavioural evidence of heavier and less disclosed use described above.

Psychological traits further complicate the story. Individuals high in Machiavellianism — a manipulative trait linked to moral flexibility — are more likely to use AI covertly, perceiving questionable academic behaviours as less unethical than their peers. The low detectability of AI-generated text weakens the deterrent effect of academic sanctions and may encourage more frequent or confident use. Perceived impunity, that is, appears to modulate actual behaviour independently of stated values.

Overall, the number of students who used AI to cheat was lower than anecdotal reports had suggested, though daily AI users had the highest rate of cheating at 26 percent, compared to 7 percent for those who used it monthly — a finding consistent with the idea that intensity of engagement with the technology, rather than mere access to it, is the critical variable. One survey found that 51 percent of students believe using AI is cheating, yet 22 percent admit they still do it — a self-reported gap that, given the behavioural evidence above, is very likely an underestimate of the actual gap.

What the evidence collectively suggests is that the academic conversation has been conducted largely in the wrong register. The salient question is not whether students cheat with AI, but rather what they actually do with it when no one is watching — and the honest methodological answer, as of mid-2026, is that research is only beginning to develop tools capable of answering that question reliably. The current body of study lacks diversity in study design and scope, often exhibits a bias toward Western contexts, and provides limited comprehensive analysis that fully balances the pedagogical benefits of generative AI against its potential for academic dishonesty. Until behavioural observation methods become more widespread, any confident claim about the true distribution of student AI use should be treated with considerable scepticism.

history.previousAnswer:
The gap between what students say they do with generative AI and what they actually do — when unobserved and unsurveyed — has become one of the more revealing and methodologically vexed problems in contemporary education research. The evidence accumulated by 2025 and 2026 cuts in several directions at once, but certain patterns are now firm enough to hold.

The headline numbers on self-reported usage are staggering on their own terms. Based on a survey of over one thousand UK undergraduates, the Higher Education Policy Institute found that the proportion of students using generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for assessments jumped from 53 percent in 2024 to 88 percent in 2025. By 2026, AI use had become nearly universal, with 95 percent of students reporting using it in at least one way and 94 percent saying they use it to help with assessed work. The Copyleaks 2025 report broadly corroborates this trajectory: nearly 90 percent of students have used AI for academic purposes, with almost a third doing so daily and another 24 percent doing so several times per week.

These are self-reported figures, however, and the distance between what students declare and what they do in practice is precisely where the more interesting research lies. The most direct evidence of systematic underreporting comes from studies using list experiments — an anonymization technique that allows respondents to admit socially stigmatized behaviors without direct attribution. A study based on interviews and list experiments with 305 Indonesian undergraduates found that students were often reluctant to admit dishonest behavior when asked directly, but the anonymous list experiment method produced substantially higher admissions of AI-assisted cheating. A comparable quantitative study of 1,386 Vietnamese undergraduates using list experiments found a similar pattern: students tended to conceal AI-assisted cheating when asked directly. The mechanism, across both contexts, appears to be shame and social pressure rather than simple ignorance of the rules.

A further dimension of the gap concerns not misconduct per se, but covert use more broadly. Qualitative research from 2026, drawing on interviews with college students, found that there is a growing misalignment between students' AI adoption and existing institutional practices — around assessment, policy, and limited AI resources — and that this misalignment has led to covert AI usage, increased student anxiety, and an intention-behavior gap where students feel pressured into disregulated AI engagement. The title of that study captures the phenomenology with precision: "Everyone's using it, but no one is allowed to talk about it." Its results show that traditional assessment structures — characterized by tight deadlines, exam stacking, and graded homework — incentivize students to use AI for task completion rather than deep engagement. In other words, institutional design is actively producing the covert behavior it nominally prohibits.

What students actually use AI *for*, when conditions allow honesty, also diverges from the catastrophizing narratives common in faculty discourse. The most common reported uses are for AI to explain concepts, summarize articles, and suggest research ideas — functions closer to an advanced reference tool than a ghost-writing service. The proportion of students directly including AI-generated text in assessed work, while rising, stands at 12 percent as of 2026, up from 8 percent in 2025 and 3 percent in 2024. This matters: even as near-universal engagement is reported, wholesale text submission remains a minority behavior. The more common, less dramatic reality is iterative assistance at earlier stages of work.

What distorts disclosure, research suggests, is not chiefly moral recklessness but institutional ambiguity. Roughly one third of respondents in one study admitted some AI use, yet disclosure was rare — and this silence appeared to reflect not dishonesty but rational caution in the face of ambiguous policies and perceived academic risk. Contrary to what institutional leaders might assume, mere awareness of a university's AI policy does little to sway student views on whether using AI is ethical; formal guidance often trails behind the informal norms students create for themselves.

The picture that emerges is thus more complicated than either the "students are cheating en masse" or "students are using AI responsibly" framings allow. Students are using generative AI far more extensively than they disclose, particularly in high-stakes assessment contexts. That concealment is shaped less by calculated dishonesty than by a policy environment that criminalizes a technology students experience as ordinary, and by assessment structures that reward speed over depth. The behavior gap, in this sense, is partly an institutional creation.
history.justification: The candidate answer introduces several materially new data points and sources not present in the stored answer: the CHI 2025 study with specific percentages on reasons for non-disclosure (fear of social judgement 54%, penalties 44%, competitive advantage 39%, etc.) and the finding that most students felt no guilt about non-disclosure; the behavioural log study of 70 undergraduates in a philosophy course finding 20% heavy AI reliance and more than half of detected users denying use; the 401-student US survey establishing that ethical beliefs (not policy awareness) are the strongest predictors of AI use; the finding that 80%+ of students at one elite liberal arts college use AI, with 61% augmentation vs 42% automation; the Machiavellianism trait finding; and the specific statistic that daily AI users cheat at 26% vs 7% for monthly users. These new empirical details extend and deepen the stored answer's conclusions without reversing them — both reach the same overall conclusion that students underreport AI use due to institutional pressure and moral reclassification, and that the self-report methodology is structurally flawed — but the candidate provides substantially richer and more specific evidentiary support.
